Step 2 — State the legal test in your own words, then list the ingredients:

Step 3 — Check limitations, provisos and the rest of the Chapter so you do not apply s. 15 in a vacuum.

learningObjectives: State the judicial-act protection in BNS s.15.
Apply the requirements that the person is a Judge, is acting judicially, and is exercising a power given by law or believed in good faith to be given by law.
Distinguish a Judge under s.15 from an officer executing a court order under s.14.
enhancement.definition: BNS s.15 provides that nothing is an offence which is done by a Judge when acting judicially in the exercise of any power which is, or which in good faith he believes to be, given to him by law.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Judicial acts of a Judge are protected when done in the exercise of a legal power, or of a power the Judge in good faith believes the law gives him. The protection is not a general immunity for every act of a person who happens to be a Judge.
statutoryFramework: Chapter III — General Exceptions, BNS s.15.
The actor must be a Judge.
The act must be done when acting judicially.
The act must be in exercise of a power given by law, or a power which in good faith the Judge believes to be given by law.
The section says nothing is an offence; it is an exception, not a sentencing discount.
Section 14 covers a person bound by law, including the statutory court-officer illustration. Section 16, if raised, is the separate provision on acts done pursuant to a judgment or order of a court.
essentialIngredients: The act is done when acting judicially.
The act is an exercise of a power.
That power is given by law, or the Judge in good faith believes it is given by law.
If any of those conditions fails, s.15 does not make the act no offence.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 15 protects the judicial function, not the private acts of a Judge. Three limits do the work. First, the actor must be a Judge. Second, the Judge must be acting judicially, so an act outside the judicial role is not covered by the section's words. Third, the act must be an exercise of a power which the law gives, or which the Judge in good faith believes the law gives. The good-faith belief branch is about the existence of the power, not about a wish to reach a particular result. A student answer should not invent a case name for this proposition. If the problem is about a warrant officer arresting the wrong person after due enquiry, that is the s.14 illustration. If the problem is about a person acting only because a court has ordered it, check the separate court-order exception rather than forcing the facts into s.15.
examples: Teaching example: a Judge, while trying a case, orders a step that the procedural law authorises. The act is done as a Judge, acting judicially, in exercise of a power given by law. Section 15 can be raised.
Teaching example: the same Judge, outside court, assaults a neighbour in a private dispute. The actor may be a Judge, but the act is not done when acting judicially. Section 15 does not apply.
Teaching example: a court officer arrests Z believing Z to be Y. Analyse s.14 illustration (b), not s.15, unless the facts separately show a Judge acting judicially.
distinctions: Section 15 is Judge-specific and requires acting judicially. Section 14 can apply to a soldier or a court officer who is bound by law.
Good faith in s.15 qualifies the belief that the power is given by law. It does not excuse a private act.
An act done merely pursuant to a judgment or order of a court is a different exception and should be cited only if that section is in play.
problemApplication: Issue: whether the act is no offence under s.15.
Rule: Judge; acting judicially; power given by law or good-faith belief that it is given by law.
Application: test each condition in order. Failure of any one ends the exception.
Conclusion: only a judicial exercise of an actual or good-faith believed legal power falls within s.15.

The power must be given by law, or believed in good faith to be given by law.
